title: Hypoalbuminemia
subject: Pathology
summary: Low serum albumin reflects poor synthesis, loss or redistribution and predicts poor outcomes. In low‑resource settings common causes include malnutrition, chronic infection and nephrotic loss.

sections.p: Serum albumin <35 g/L measured by standard laboratory assay. Diagnosis requires a reliable blood sample and exclusion of lab error.
b: Albumin is the main plasma protein, maintaining oncotic pressure and transporting hormones, drugs and fatty acids.
Low albumin is a marker of chronic disease, malnutrition or loss.

sections.p: Clinical staging correlates with serum level and presence of edema or organ dysfunction.
b: Mild: 30‑34 g/L, usually asymptomatic.
Moderate: 20‑29 g/L, may have peripheral edema.
Severe: <20 g/L, risk of ascites, pleural effusion, impaired drug binding.

sections.p: Identify whether albumin loss, decreased synthesis or redistribution is dominant.
b: Malnutrition (protein‑energy deficiency) – most common in low‑resource settings.
Chronic infections: HIV, TB, chronic hepatitis B/C, malaria.
Nephrotic syndrome – urinary loss of albumin.
Protein‑losing enteropathy (e.g., intestinal parasites, inflammatory bowel disease).
Liver cirrhosis – impaired synthesis.
Acute phase response – redistribution to the interstitium.

sections.p: Patients may appear thin, with peripheral edema, ascites, or pleural effusion; drug toxicity can increase because of reduced binding.
b: Pitting edema of ankles.
Shifting dullness on abdominal exam for ascites.
Low blood pressure or tachycardia if intravascular volume falls.

t.b: Assess synthetic capacity; low albumin with elevated transaminases suggests hepatic disease.
Detects urinary loss; >3 g/24 h points to nephrotic syndrome.
Looks for protein‑losing enteropathy; positive results guide treatment.
Identify chronic infection or inflammation contributing to redistribution.
Use clinical signs (edema, ascites) and surrogate markers like total protein; treat presumptively while arranging referral.

sections.p: Severe hypoalbuminemia can precipitate circulatory collapse, pulmonary edema, and drug toxicity.
b: Rapidly falling blood pressure.
New‑onset dyspnea with crackles – possible pulmonary edema.
Signs of bleeding due to reduced oncotic support of vascular wall.

sections.p: Treat underlying cause, provide nutritional support, and monitor fluid status. Albumin infusion is reserved for specific emergencies.
b: Nutritional rehabilitation: high‑protein diet, oral supplements; consider therapeutic feeding programs.
Treat infections: antiretrovirals for HIV, anti‑TB regimen, antimalarials as indicated.
Nephrotic syndrome: ACE‑inhibitor or ARB to reduce proteinuria; diuretics for edema.
Liver disease: address viral hepatitis, avoid hepatotoxins, consider referral for advanced care.
Albumin infusion (20 g/L solution) only for hypotension unresponsive to fluids, severe ascites with diuretic resistance, or peri‑operative support.

sections.p: Regular monitoring of albumin and clinical status; address socioeconomic factors that perpetuate malnutrition.
b: Re‑measure albumin every 2‑4 weeks until stable.
Screen household for food insecurity; involve community nutrition programs.
Vaccinate against hepatitis B, provide insecticide‑treated nets to reduce malaria.

sections.p: Conditions that cause edema but have normal albumin.
b: Congestive heart failure – edema from hydrostatic pressure, albumin usually normal.
Nephritic syndrome – protein loss is modest; albumin often >30 g/L.

sections.p: Factors that falsely elevate or lower measured albumin.
b: Dehydration concentrates serum proteins, giving a spuriously high albumin.
Acute phase response can lower albumin without true loss; interpret with CRP.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden drop in blood pressure despite fluids
Rapidly expanding abdominal girth with tense ascites

faq.a: Inflammatory cytokines shift albumin from the intravascular to the interstitial space and suppress hepatic synthesis.

faq.q: Can I give albumin to any patient with low levels?
faq.a: No; albumin is costly and only indicated for specific circulatory or oncotic emergencies.

faq.q: How does low albumin affect drug dosing?
faq.a: Drugs that bind albumin (e.g., warfarin, phenytoin) have higher free fractions, increasing efficacy and toxicity; adjust monitoring accordingly.

exam: A 45‑year‑old man with HIV presents with peripheral edema and albumin 22 g/L. What is your next diagnostic step? — Check urine protein to rule out nephrotic loss before starting nutrition.

How would you differentiate hypoalbuminemia from congestive heart failure in a patient with ankle swelling? — Look for elevated JVP, pulmonary crackles, and normal albumin; hypoalbuminemia shows low albumin and may have ascites without cardiac signs.
Why is albumin infusion contraindicated in uncomplicated malnutrition? — It does not correct the underlying protein deficit and may cause fluid overload; focus on dietary rehabilitation.
A patient on warfarin develops a serum albumin of 18 g/L. How does this affect anticoagulation? — Free warfarin fraction rises, increasing INR; monitor more frequently and consider dose adjustment.
What red‑flag symptom would prompt immediate transfer to a higher‑level facility? — Sudden hypotension unresponsive to fluids indicating possible circulatory collapse.
In a setting without albumin assay, what clinical sign reliably suggests severe hypoalbuminemia? — Pitting edema with shifting dullness indicating ascites plus low total protein.
Explain why chronic hepatitis B can cause hypoalbuminemia. — Ongoing hepatocellular injury impairs albumin synthesis despite preserved liver size.
What is the first‑line nutritional intervention for a child with protein‑energy malnutrition and albumin 28 g/L? — Ready‑to‑use therapeutic food (RUTF) providing high‑quality protein and calories.
